one_liner: Embedded C key-value store for NVMe SSDs; paper reports 6-10x RocksDB insert throughput and 2-2.6x point-query throughput.
what_it_does: SplinterDB is a Linux-only embedded, ordered key-value store written in C and linked as a library (make install produces libsplinterdb.so and .a). The C API in include/splinterdb/splinterdb.h covers create/open/close on a file or block device, insert, delete, update (blind merge messages defined by a user data_config), point lookup with a 'might exist' mode, and bounded forward/backward iterators. The iterator is modeled on RocksDB's, but it is not a drop-in: the start key is fixed at iterator init (no Seek), and there are no column families, WriteBatch or transactions.
how_it_is_fast: The core structure is the STBε-tree (size-tiered Bε-tree): a trunk tree of fanout 8-16 whose nodes point to immutable B-tree 'branches', each paired with a quotient filter instead of a Bloom filter. Size-tiering plus a flush-then-compact policy rewrite each key fewer times than leveled LSM compaction (about half RocksDB's write amplification in the paper) and let many small, local compactions run in parallel. A concurrent memtable (hand-over-hand locking) and a user-level clock cache with distributed reader-writer locks and O_DIRECT I/O remove the CPU and lock contention that, per the paper, holds RocksDB to about 30% of an Optane SSD's bandwidth.
when_to_use: Write-heavy ingest of small pairs (paper: 24B keys, 100B values) on fast NVMe, where RocksDB is CPU-bound rather than device-bound
Datasets far larger than RAM (paper caps memory at about 10% of the dataset, 4GiB) that still need fast point lookups
Many-threaded clients: the paper reports point reads at 18.5x single-thread throughput with 24 threads (YCSB C)
Workloads that can express changes as blind updates (append, increment) through a custom data_config, skipping read-modify-write
Research systems or prototypes on Linux that can accept an unstable API and unversioned on-disk format
when_not_to_use: Data that must survive a crash: the write-ahead log is off unless use_log is set, there is no fsync/commit API, and core_mount still says crash recovery (log replay + allocator rebuild) is not wired, so a database that was not cleanly closed refuses to mount
Short range scans on small values: the paper measured YCSB E about 15% slower than RocksDB with 100B values (about 15% faster with 1KiB values)
Anything needing transactions/atomic multi-put, range delete, a stable API, or an on-disk format that survives upgrades (all listed in docs/limitations.md)
Non-Linux targets: macOS and Windows are unsupported because the I/O layer is built on libaio

Long-running production ingest before re-testing: open issues #560 (critical assert in routing_filter_add on large small-pair insert runs, 2023) and #585 (segfault in routing_filter_lookup under YCSB-C) have no recorded resolution

integration.dependencies: libaio, libxxhash, pthread, libm (build docs also install libconfig-dev)
integration.min_toolchain: C with GNU extensions; minimum version not documented; CI uses GCC 13 and Clang 19; public headers are C++-compatible (extern "C")
integration.platforms: Linux only; CI runs on x86-64 Ubuntu; the Makefile adds -march=native on x86-64 and skips it elsewhere, but aarch64 support is not documented or tested
integration.thread_safety: One splinterdb handle is designed for concurrent use by many threads, which auto-register on first call; only one process may open a database file/device; a lookup_result object must not be shared across threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — iterator semantics mirror RocksDB's, but it is a different C API with no Seek, column families, WriteBatch, transactions or options compatibility

gotchas: The default release build uses -O3 -ffast-math -flto and, on x86-64, -march=native, so a library built on one machine can fault on an older CPU
cache_size and data_config (key compare, merge functions) are not stored in the database and must be supplied identically on every open; disk size is fixed at create time
Iterators must be deinitialized; the header warns a live iterator can block inserts, deletes and close from the same thread
docs/limitations.md lags the code: it still says keys and values must be smaller than the 4KiB page, but PR #674 (May 2026) added values larger than a page
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SplinterDB for write-heavy, small-pair ordered workloads on NVMe when you can accept an experimental engine with weak crash safety; choose TerarkDB or Titan to stay RocksDB-compatible (Titan for large values), libmdbx for read-mostly ACID transactions, and NuDB for append-only insert/fetch with no ordering.
verified_claims_summary: The USENIX ATC'20 paper replayed YCSB-derived traces (load and A-F, 24B keys, 100B and 1KiB values) against an unnamed version of RocksDB (and PebblesDB) on a Dell R720 with a 32-core 2.0 GHz Xeon and an Optane 905p SSD, memory capped at 4GiB by a cgroup: SplinterDB was 6-10x faster on inserts, 2-2.6x on point queries, roughly equal on short scans, with half the write amplification. Compiler and flags were not reported; the repo's tests/functional/ycsb_test.c is a SplinterDB trace replayer, but the traces and the RocksDB side of the harness are not in the repo.
status_note: Actively developed by VMware Research (values larger than a page, async scans and checkpointing all landed in 2026) under Apache-2.0, but there are no releases and the maintainers say it is not for production before 1.0.
